Grace: Hi, Arnold! Good to see you! Are you doing a Toastmaster's speech tonight? I can't remember if I saw your name on the program.
Arnold: Yes, I am. I want to warm up a bit. Do you want to hear a run-through of my speech?
Grace: Sure, I would love to hear it!
Arnold: I'm going to talk about the value of procrastinating.
Grace: Really?
Arnold: Yes. I'm a total believer in procrastinating. It's become a matter of principle for me.
Grace: I wonder if I should listen to your speech.

Arnold: You've been brought up to think procrastinating is bad. That's because other people have been deciding what is important for you to do, according to their own priorities. Procrastinating means deciding for yourself which tasks you can leave till the last minute. It doesn't mean not doing them, it just means waiting until you have more information to complete the task efficiently.
Grace: I worry about what happens if I don't have time to get everything done.
Arnold: Procrastinators like me believe that one of the main principles of success is doing things quickly, not perfectly. The law of diminishing returns says that after a certain point of making an effort, the amount you get back becomes smaller and smaller. In my view, trying to be perfect is very inefficient.

Grace: I'm not sure if this is connected to procrastinating.
Arnold: Yes, it is. Procrastinators are of the opinion that the task will be done faster, and therefore more efficiently, when you are closer to the deadline. You can also avoid a lot of problems caused by changing circumstances.
Grace: OK, I'll listen to your speech, but I'm not going to promise to become a procrastinator!

You can use whether or if when you want to talk about a situation where there are two possibilities or choices.

If you can ask a yes/no question, then it's usually possible to use whether or if.
I don't know if/whether she's single.
(The question here would be: Is she single?)
You usually use whether when you are talking about a situation with different choices.

Let's compare the following sentences.
Let me know whether you need a ticket for the concert.
(Here, the alternatives are “you need a ticket” or “you don't need a ticket”. You should let me know in either case.)

Let me know if you need a ticket for the concert.
(This sentence presents a condition. Only tell me if you need a ticket. This sentence is not grammatically incorrect, it just presents a different idea from the one above.)

You use if more often when there is a noun clause in the sentence as the object of the verb.
Laura wasn't sure if how she answered the question was wrong.
I can't remember if I saw your name on the program.
I wonder if I should listen to your speech.
You can use different modal verbs to show intention. Intention means your aim or purpose, something that you plan or want to do.
There are many times when you want to talk about or discuss things you intend to do. This could be as simple as plans for the weekend or goals you want to achieve.
You can use the following words to express these intentions.

You can also make questions to ask about someone's intentions.

Examples:
Will you take a vacation this month or at the end of the year?
How do you think you are going to celebrate New Year's Eve?
Would you like to go to the museum with me?
What do you want to do on the weekend?
